episodes.request: Someone on the editor team asked how autosave-sim decides when drafts are saved, and what the keystroke log format is. Can you explain it from the code? No changes, please.

steps.thought: The README describes the simulator and the log format; start there.
steps.output:
# notes-autosave

The autosave timing of the notes editor: `debounce` and `throttle` helpers that run
on an injectable scheduler, the draft autosave that saves a field of a note once
typing pauses, and `autosave-sim`, a simulator that replays a keystroke log and prints
when drafts would be saved, for tuning the delays.

## Autosave

    import { createAutosave } from "./src/autosave.ts";

    const autosave = createAutosave({
      noteId: "n-1042",
      field: "body",
      save: (draft) => drafts.put(draft), // { noteId, field, text, revision }
    });
    editor.on("input", () => autosave.edit(editor.text));
    editor.on("close", () => autosave.flush());

Each field of a note (`title`, `body`, `tags`, `checklist`) has its own autosave. A
draft is saved once the user pauses typing for the field's wait (1000 ms for every
field), with the text after the last edit; `revision` counts the edits of the field
since the note was opened. The title is also saved at the first edit of a burst, so
that the note list shows the new title at once. `flush()` saves the last edit at once
if it is still waiting (the editor calls it when a note is closed), `pending()` says
whether an edit is waiting, and `dispose()` drops it. `delays: { wait, maxWait }`
replaces the field's delays; the simulator and the tests use it.

## Timing helpers

`debounce(fn, wait, options, scheduler)` returns a function that runs `fn` once calls
pause for `wait` milliseconds:

- calls less than `wait` apart form a burst, and `fn` runs once, `wait` ms after the
  last call of the burst, with the arguments of that last call;
- `leading: true` also runs `fn` at the first call of a burst; it then runs again at
  the end only if more calls came during the wait;
- `maxWait` ends a burst that goes on longer than that: `fn` runs with the arguments
  of the last call, and the next call starts a new burst;
- `trailing: false` does not run `fn` at the end of a burst;
- the returned function has `cancel()`, `flush()` (run the waiting call now), and
  `pending()` (whether a call is waiting).

`throttle(fn, interval, options, scheduler)` runs `fn` at most once per interval: a
call outside an interval at once, and the last call made during an interval when the
interval ends (not with `trailing: false`). The editor's scroll sync uses it.

Both take a `Scheduler` (`now`, `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`); the default is the real
clock. `ManualScheduler` is a scheduler whose time moves only when `advance(ms)`,
`advanceTo(time)`, or `runAll()` is called, for the tests and the simulator. A delay
that is negative or not a finite number throws a `RangeError`.

## Simulator

    node --experimental-strip-types bin/autosave-sim.ts examples/typing.txt
    node --experimental-strip-types bin/autosave-sim.ts --field title examples/typing.txt
    node --experimental-strip-types bin/autosave-sim.ts --wait 600 --max-wait 3000 examples/typing.txt
    npm run sim -- examples/typing.txt

A keystroke log has one event per line, with the time in whole milliseconds from the
start:

    # Ada starts a shopping list
    0 type M
    110 type Mi
    3900 close

`TIME type TEXT` is an edit, where TEXT is the whole text of the field after the edit,
and `TIME close` closes the note. Times must not go down. Blank lines and lines
starting with `#` are skipped.

The simulator replays the log through the autosave of `--field` (default `body`) and
prints the delays, one line per saved draft (the time, the revision, and the text),
and a summary. `--wait MS` and `--max-wait MS` replace the field's delays:

    $ node --experimental-strip-types bin/autosave-sim.ts --wait 800 examples/typing.txt
    autosave of body (wait 800 ms)
      1320 ms  saved r5 "Milk,"
      3900 ms  saved r9 "Milk, eggs"
    9 edits, 2 saves

A log line that cannot be read, a file that cannot be read, and a command line that
autosave-sim does not understand stop it with a message on stderr and exit status 2.

## Development

    npm test

There are no dependencies: the code is TypeScript run directly by Node 22 with
`--experimental-strip-types`, and the tests use `node:test`.

steps.thought: The log is read in src/keystrokes.ts.
The replay itself is in src/simulate.ts.

finish.thought: The simulator only moves time and records saves; the autosave decides when to save.
finish.report: parseKeystrokes in src/keystrokes.ts reads one event per line: `TIME type TEXT` is an edit, where TEXT is the whole text of the field after the edit (it may be empty and keeps its spaces), and `TIME close` closes the note. TIME is whole milliseconds from the start and must not go down. Blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped; any other line, or a time that goes down, throws a KeystrokeError that names the line, and autosave-sim reports it with exit status 2. simulate in src/simulate.ts makes a ManualScheduler and the autosave of the chosen field (body by default), with the delays from --wait and --max-wait or, without them, the autosave's own delays (1000 ms for every field, as the README says). For each event it first moves time to the event with advanceTo, so a save that comes due before the event happens first; then an edit goes to autosave.edit and a close to autosave.flush. After the last event, runAll lets every waiting save happen. Each save is recorded with the time it happened, and formatSimulation prints the delays, one line per saved draft (time, revision, and text), and a count of edits and saves. So the simulator does not decide when a draft is saved: the autosave and its debounce do, and the simulator only moves time and records the saves.

episodes.request: What does ManualScheduler do when two timers are due at the same time, or when a timer sets another timer while time is moving?

steps.thought: See where the simulator moves time.

finish.thought: advanceTo looks for the next due timer again after every run, which answers both questions.
finish.report: ManualScheduler in src/scheduler.ts keeps its timers with their due time and an id that goes up with every setTimeout. advanceTo(time) repeatedly takes the next timer due at or before the target time: the one due earliest and, of timers due at the same time, the one with the lowest id, which is the one that was set first. It removes that timer, sets the current time to its due time, and runs it; at the end the time is set to the target. Because it looks for the next due timer again after every run, a timer that a callback sets while time is moving runs in the same move when it comes due by the target time. advance(ms) is advanceTo(now + ms), and moving time back, or by a negative or NaN amount, throws a RangeError. runAll keeps moving to the next due timer until none is left and gives up with an error after 10000 moves, for timers that keep setting new timers. The simulator calls advanceTo once per event and runAll after the last one.

episodes.request: Last question: how many tests cover throttle, the scheduler, and the keystroke logs?

steps.thought: The test files use top-level test() calls, so counting those lines counts the tests.

finish.report: 16 tests: 4 in test/throttle.test.ts (a call outside an interval, the last call of an interval, trailing: false, and cancel), 7 in test/scheduler.test.ts (the start time, due order, timers due at the same time, cleared timers, timers set while time moves, runAll and moving time back, and checkDelay), and 5 in test/keystrokes.test.ts (edits and closes, spaces and empty text, comments and blank lines, bad lines, and times that go down).
